|---|---|---|

### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Chin and Chen give the field its first joint, quasi-experimental look at how Indiana's 2011 voucher-plus-charter-authorizer expansion affected district finances, operational inputs, local property-tax referenda, and district-level achievement, using a within-county difference-in-differences design with a baseline-predicted "choice exposure" index as treatment. The paper is unusually transparent — eleven specifications in Table 2, candid limitation-writing, and a self-reported conflicting study — and its best-supported findings can be relied on: districts predicted to be most exposed cut per-pupil expenditures (direction robust across every specification, magnitude somewhere between roughly \$160 and \$520 per pupil depending on the comparison group, and not significant once comparison districts are reweighted or bordering districts dropped), raised student-to-FTE-teacher ratios by about half a student, and held and passed more property-tax referenda, chiefly for capital projects. But the paper's most quotable claims are its least supported. The local-revenue mechanism that anchors the abstract's political-economy story is significant in only one of eleven specifications and positive in two; the claim that referenda "could not commensurately counteract" revenue losses is inferred from two separate models, never estimated; the achievement "reversal" rests on two pre-treatment years of district-mean SEDA data that cannot separate district effects from compositional change, and student-level Indiana work (Adger & Felegi 2024) finds the opposite sign; and the 2011 lapse of ARRA and levy-replacement funds — which fell hardest on exactly the larger, poorer districts the exposure index labels treated — is described in the paper's own context section but never tested as a confound. Read this as credible evidence on how Indiana's high-exposure districts adjusted spending and staffing after 2011 and as an agenda-setting first look at school choice and local tax politics; do not read it as settled evidence that choice reduces local revenues, weakens voter support for taxation, or lowers student achievement.

#### Key Strengths

- **A clean shock and a defensible dosage design.** Indiana's 2011 double reform has a single implementation date, so the staggered-DD pathologies genuinely do not apply, and the authors' elastic-net-predicted exposure index (built only from 2009-10 baseline covariates, jackknife-stable, with a first-stage in Appendix Figure A2) avoids defining treatment by post-policy uptake that is endogenous to district decisions.
- **Robustness reported with rare candor.** Table 2 prints eleven specifications — including the two (M10 inverse-propensity reweighting and M11 non-bordering comparisons) that attenuate the headline expenditure effect by 60-70% — and the text openly shows the estimated linear pre-trend flipping sign across 3-, 6-, and 9-year pre-windows. The county-by-year fixed effects and the honest disclosure of the effective sample (42 counties, 177 districts) are further marks of care.
- **A genuinely new outcome.** Hand-assembled, cross-verified Indiana referendum records brought into a causal design are without close precedent in the school-choice literature, and the capital-versus-operational split — exposed districts win levies for buildings but not for instruction — is a specific, policy-relevant fact that survives the demanding first-referendum-only restriction.
- **The whole causal chain in one setting.** Estimating finance, inputs, and achievement under one design and one treatment definition lets the paper speak to the Figure 1 mechanism chain rather than a single link, which few prior fiscal-spillover studies (Buerger & Bifulco, Mann & Bruno, Ridley & Terrier) manage.
- **Limitations stated, not performed.** The Conclusion names the SEDA composition problem, the rho ~ .75 correlation that prevents separating voucher from charter exposure, the mismatch between CES federal-spending items and local tax attitudes, and the cross-district enrollment problem, and it volunteers the contradicting Adger & Felegi (2024) result. The Indiana finance-context section is itself valuable institutional scholarship.

#### Key Concerns

- **An untested confound sits on top of the treatment definition.** Treated districts are, by construction, Indiana's larger, poorer, more urban, more heavily Black districts (Table 1: 6,513 vs. 2,096 students; \$979 vs. \$618 baseline federal revenue per pupil). ARRA funds and the 2008 circuit-breaker's levy-replacement grants both expired in 2011 on poverty- and tax-rate gradients that track that index; the federal-revenue decline in Panel E is exactly what a poverty-graded funding cliff produces. M6 (linear time trends by two demographic medians) is only a partial answer, and no honest-DD-style bound is reported.
- **The prose outruns Table 2.** The text calls results "generally robust in direction, magnitude, and statistical significance," but total expenditures fall from -\$521 (M4) to -\$201 and -\$161 (ns) in M10/M11; local revenue (Panel G) is significant only in the simple DD and positive in M2/M3; capital outlays are significant in one column; schools-in-operation in one. The Conclusion's "primarily driven by fewer dollars being received through local sources" is not what its own preferred specification shows.
- **The achievement result is the paper's most fragile and most citable claim.** Only two pre-treatment years exist, the post-period pattern is a monotone drift rather than a discrete reversal, district-mean SEDA scores confound district productivity with composition, the six subgroups are nested samples in the same districts, the largest negative estimates coincide with Indiana's 2015 and 2019 assessment transitions, and student-level work on the same reform finds improvement.
- **The referenda-versus-revenue "insufficiency" story is asserted, not estimated.** No exhibit puts levy dollars raised against appropriations lost. The +21pp/+12pp headline figures come from an "ever held / ever passed" DD that compares a ~2-year pre-window to an 8-year post-window and cannot show pre-trends; the paper's own event-study version gives +5pp (any) and +4pp (capital), and the stated-preference evidence that rescues the theory (CES, Appendix D) asks about Congress and represents state adults.
- **Reproducibility gaps and expository errors that readers will trip over.** No data availability statement, code, or software environment; unstated deflator and sample-inclusion rules; observation counts that do not follow from the stated panel; an Equation 4 time-centering contradiction (2011 vs. Year - 2012); a p. 17 significance claim contradicted by Figures 5 and 7; a broken abstract sentence; a Figure 2 with two contradictory legends; a "class size" label for a student-to-FTE ratio; and mangled reference entries (Jackson, Johnson & Persico; Ridley & Terrier; Friedman; Mann & Bruno's year).

#### What to Rely On

- Indiana districts with high predicted exposure to the 2011 choice expansion reduced per-pupil expenditures, particularly current (instructional) outlays, relative to low-exposure districts in the same county. The direction holds in all eleven specifications; treat the magnitude as a range (roughly -\$160 to -\$520 per pupil in the parametric models; up to ~\$680, or ~6.4% of baseline, at the 2019 endpoint of the event study) rather than a point.
- Student-to-FTE-teacher ratios rose in those districts by roughly half a student per teacher. The 2010-to-2012 jump is about ten times what the pre-trend slope predicts, and the effect survives the continuous-dose, IPW, and non-bordering checks (though it is borderline in M6-M8).
- High-exposure districts held and passed more property-tax referenda after 2011, and that effect is concentrated in capital rather than operational levies; the capital effect survives the first-referendum-only restriction (+11pp, significant) while the operational effect does not (+3pp).
- Predicted exposure to choice is a real dosage: the index predicts actual uptake only after 2011 (Appendix Figure A2), and 35% vs. 12% of public schools in treated vs. comparison districts sit within five miles of a charter or private school.
- The paper is the appropriate reference point for Indiana's 2011 voucher-plus-charter-authorizer bundle and for the argument that fiscal effects of choice are state-specific and must be estimated separately by finance system.
- The methodological point that a parametric linear event study would have masked the non-monotonic achievement pattern (and that pre-trend tests are window-dependent) is correct and well demonstrated.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- **"Revenue losses were primarily driven by local sources."** Local revenue (Table 2 Panel G) is significant only in the simple DD (M1), positive in M2 and M3, and -\$125.8 (SE 141.2) in the preferred M4; the Figure 7 pattern is partly the continuation of a large positive-to-zero pre-trend.
- **"Districts could not commensurately counteract shrinking revenues through referenda."** This is an inference across two separately estimated models; the paper never quantifies levy dollars raised against revenue lost, and the total-revenue estimate it depends on is itself window-dependent (ns in M3, significant in M4/M5).
- **"Short-term achievement gains reversed and became substantially negative."** Two pre-years, district-mean SEDA outcomes that mix district effects with composition, 90% intervals, a widest-interval 2019 endpoint that coincides with the ILEARN transition, and an opposite-signed student-level study (Adger & Felegi 2024) on the same reform.
- **"School choice weakens voter preferences for taxation."** The revealed-preference result points the other way (more referenda held and passed); the weakening-preferences reading rests on exploratory CES items about federal spending that the authors themselves say not to over-read.
- **Any statement about vouchers specifically.** The exposure index correlates .98 with predicted charter growth and .84 with predicted voucher uptake, so this is closer to charter-exposure evidence; the "conservative for vouchers" argument is theoretical, not tested.
- **The -2.4% housing-value mechanism, the 8/3/11pp first-referendum figures, and the school-proximity statistics.** All appear only in prose with no standard errors, sample sizes, or exhibits; the housing-value ACS-to-LEA geocoding is undescribed.
- **The p. 17 claim that pre-2011 coefficients "contain zero" and post-2011 coefficients "do not."** Figure 5's 2007 current-expenditure coefficient (+258) and Figure 7's 2006 revenue coefficients (+504, +521) have 90% CIs excluding zero; the paper's own p. 25 acknowledges a significant -\$45/year current-expenditure pre-trend.
- **The sample size.** Cite 177 districts (99 comparison, 78 treatment) in 42 counties — the effective sample disclosed on p. 31 — not the 287 in Table 1; and cite "class size" as a student-to-FTE-teacher ratio, which is what Figure 6 actually plots.
- **Generalization beyond Indiana.** The estimand is a within-county contrast between larger, poorer districts and their small rural neighbors under Indiana's circuit-breaker, referendum-gated finance system and its 2011 collective-bargaining restrictions (which removed class size from bargaining — the paper's clearest input margin). The authors flag this; readers in ESA/voucher-only states should not transport the estimates.

## Codex synthesis

### Overall Assessment: Useful With Caveats

Chin and Chen provide useful Indiana-specific evidence that districts with greater predicted exposure to the combined voucher and charter expansion experienced relative declines in per-pupil spending, increases in student-to-teacher ratios, increased cumulative referendum activity, and an early improvement followed by deterioration in aggregate achievement (Figures 5–9, pp. 18–20, 27, 29). The contribution is strongest in bringing fiscal adjustment, staffing, and local revenue-raising efforts into the same empirical account. My judgment is that these patterns warrant selective citation, with causal attribution conditional on parallel trends and the absence of differential contemporaneous shocks. Published sensitivity checks support the direction of expenditure and staffing changes more consistently than their precise magnitudes or a predominantly local-revenue explanation (Table 2, pp. 23–24). The paper does not establish that individual tax preferences weakened, that spending cuts caused learning losses for the same students, or that vouchers alone produced the findings. The adequate methods, literature, and contribution assessments are compatible with weak writing and reproducibility assessments: inspectable evidence retains value, while reporting discrepancies, ambiguous exposure construction, and unavailable supplementary analyses prevent unqualified reliance on the headline interpretation.

#### Key Strengths

- A substantively useful combination of district finances, operational inputs, referendum outcomes, and aggregate achievement broadens the study beyond enrollment or test scores alone; its distinctive contribution is the joint fiscal and electoral account (pp. 3–5, 10–12; Figures 5–9, pp. 18–20, 27, 29).
- The within-county difference-in-differences design includes district and county-by-year fixed effects, predicts exposure using baseline characteristics, and clusters standard errors by district. These are meaningful safeguards against stable district differences, shared local shocks, and direct reliance on realized enrollment losses, although they do not guarantee exogenous exposure (pp. 12–15).
- Dynamic plots and a substantial published sensitivity table allow readers to inspect timing, uncertainty, and variation across specifications. The tabulated post-period expenditure coefficients remain negative and student-to-teacher coefficients positive across the reported specifications, although significance varies and the dosage specification uses a different scale (Table 2, pp. 23–24, panels A and H; model definitions, pp. 22–25).
- The literature and institutional discussion recognize fiscal-spillover predecessors and context-dependent effects; the conclusion explicitly acknowledges student composition, survey limitations, the combined policy treatment, and cross-district exposure. This supports treating the paper as a contextual extension of existing research (pp. 3–6, 8–10, 31–34).

#### Key Concerns

- Causal identification remains contestable. Exposure predictors track baseline demographic and institutional differences, and finance and staffing exhibits show pre-policy movement (Table 1, p. 16; Figures 5–7, pp. 18–20). County-by-year effects cannot remove differential district-level exposure to the concurrent funding and labor changes described on pp. 10 and 22. The trend specification that sets time to zero after reform does not extrapolate the untreated pre-trend into the post period (p. 22); my judgment is that its sensitivity results do not settle the parallel-trends concern.
- Fiscal robustness is outcome-specific. Against the statement that results are 'generally robust in direction, magnitude, and statistical significance' (p. 26), Table 2 reports total-spending coefficients of '−521.3***' in M4, '−201.1' in M10, and '−161.1' in M11 (p. 23, panel A), and local-revenue coefficients of '−297.1***' in M1 versus '72.29' in M3 (p. 24, panel G). The latter spending estimates are smaller and unstarred, and local revenue changes sign. Samples and specifications differ, so these comparisons weaken claims of stable magnitude and mechanism without proving no effect.
- The political-preference mechanism is indirect: holding and holding-and-passing referenda combine district decisions, proposal terms, repeated attempts, turnout, and voter choices (Figure 8, p. 27; Note 7, p. 37). Cumulative outcomes also involve unequal pre/post opportunity windows (p. 28). Neither these outcomes nor their coexistence with falling revenues identifies changing individual attitudes or the dollars by which referendum receipts offset losses; the separate survey evidence is exploratory and locally imprecise (pp. 27–28, 31).
- The achievement series follows changing district populations, and the staffing outcome is students per full-time-equivalent teacher rather than observed classroom enrollment (pp. 10–12, 32; Figures 6 and 9, pp. 19, 29). My judgment is that the common trajectory across outcomes is consistent with a spending-to-learning mechanism but does not identify it; subgroup analyses do not remove selection within subgroups.
- Reporting and reconstruction problems affect central measures. The exposure prose says 'ratio of charter and voucher students to traditional public school students (at baseline),' whereas Equation 3 includes 'ncharter_it + nvoucher_it + ntps_i,2010' in the denominator (p. 14; equation transcribed). The implemented construction cannot be resolved from the article. Data assembly, tuning, and assignment details are incomplete, and the supplied PDF provides no explicit replication-package location; its online supplements are not bound into the PDF and were unavailable (pp. 10–15, 35–37). These are barriers to verification, not evidence that no package exists elsewhere.

#### What to Rely On

- Conditional evidence of relative fiscal and staffing adjustment in more-exposed Indiana districts: per-pupil spending falls and student-to-teacher ratios rise in the published main estimates, with greater consistency in direction than precision across sensitivity checks (Figures 5–6, pp. 18–19; Table 2, pp. 23–24, panels A and H).
- Evidence of increased cumulative local revenue-raising activity: the estimated changes are 21 percentage points for holding any referendum and 12 percentage points for holding and passing one, with clearer passage evidence for capital than operational referenda (Figure 8, p. 27). These are district-period outcomes, not approval rates conditional on a vote (p. 28; Note 7, p. 37), and causal interpretation retains the design caveats.
- A reversal in the published aggregate achievement trajectory: early positive relative estimates become negative later, with the all-student endpoint labeled −0.097 effect-size units (Figure 9, p. 29). This can be cited as a pattern in district averages, with the paper's explicit composition qualification (p. 32).
- An Indiana-specific contribution connecting school-choice exposure, fiscal adjustment, and electoral responses within an established literature; the paper itself explains why funding arrangements and collective bargaining can condition applicability elsewhere (pp. 3–6, 8–10, 31).

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- Precise causal spending losses and a predominantly local-revenue or school-closure mechanism: published sensitivity estimates attenuate, lose significance, or change sign, depending on the outcome; nonparallel trends and differential concurrent shocks remain plausible (Table 2, pp. 23–24, panels A, G, and I; pp. 10, 21–26).
- Claims that choice weakened individual support for taxation or public goods: referendum occurrences do not isolate preferences, and the unavailable survey appendix cannot independently corroborate that mechanism here (Figure 8, p. 27; pp. 28, 31; Note 7, p. 37).
- Claims of larger actual classes, learning losses for a fixed student population, or achievement damage caused by spending cuts: the measures are staffing ratios and repeated district averages, with no identified mediation pathway (pp. 10–12, 32; Figures 6 and 9, pp. 19, 29).
- Voucher-only effects, a statewide effect of choice versus no choice, or predictions for other states: the comparison is greater versus lower predicted exposure to combined reforms, with cross-district measurement error and institution-dependent responses (pp. 13–15, 31, 33–34). The study does not adjudicate school choice's general benefits or costs across all school sectors.
- Exact reproducibility and appendix-based assurances about achievement robustness, annual referendum outcomes, or stated preferences: the supplied article leaves consequential implementation details unresolved and those supplementary exhibits are unavailable. Neither a completed replication nor a failure to replicate has been demonstrated (pp. 14, 27–30, 35–37).

#### Verification notes

- CONFIRMED — Methods/contribution/writing: Table 2 gives total spending as −521.3 (SE 187.2) in M4, −201.1 (131.2) in M10, and −161.1 (163.8) in M11; the latter estimates are unstarred (p. 23, panel A).
- CONFIRMED — Methods/contribution/writing: local revenue is −297.1 (SE 110.6) in M1 and +72.29 (136.4) in M3; only M1's post-period coefficient is starred in that panel (p. 24, Table 2, panel G).
- CONFIRMED — Writing: p. 17 says finance differences are 'significant only after 2011'; Figure 5 labels the pre-policy current-expenditure estimate '258' for 2007 and its displayed 90% interval excludes zero (p. 18). This alone refutes the categorical statement, without proving the design invalid.
- CONFIRMED — Writing: p. 15 says 'only the number of private schools appears to vary' among selected predictors after county adjustment; Table 1 also reports 'Enrollment: Proportion Black' at adjusted difference '0.06' and 'Proportion single mom' at '0.07', each with rounded p value '.00' (p. 16; selected predictors, p. 14).
- CONFIRMED — Writing/reproducibility: the exposure prose and Equation 3 use different denominators (p. 14; quoted under Key Concerns); the rendered equation includes charter and voucher enrollment as well as baseline traditional-public enrollment.
- CONFIRMED — Contribution/methods: Figure 8 labels any-referendum holding '.21' and passage '.12' (p. 27); Note 7 codes both failed votes and no vote as zero for passage (p. 37), confirming the unconditional district outcome.
- CONFIRMED — Methods: the final all-student estimate is −0.097 effect-size units (p. 29, Figure 9); Note 8 uses assessment-weighted district-grade-subject means, and p. 32 explicitly acknowledges compositional change (p. 37).
- COULD NOT CHECK — Supplement-dependent claims about annual referendum checks, achievement robustness, stated preferences, and complete replication materials cannot be verified from the supplied PDF (pp. 27–30, 35–37); the literature review's external-source comparisons were not independently rechecked or used as established findings in this synthesis.
